expectedText:
GUARDIAN AD LITEM APPOINTMENT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jane Doe · John Smith

WHEN A GUARDIAN AD LITEM MUST OR MAY BE APPOINTED
Under California Code of Civil Procedure § 372(a)(1), when Alex Doe is a minor, a person who lacks legal capacity to make decisions, or a person for whom a conservator has been appointed and is a party to a civil action or proceeding, Alex Doe must appear either through a guardian or conservator of the estate or through a guardian ad litem appointed by the court in which the action or proceeding is pending, or by a judge of that court. Separately, § 372(a)(2)(A) lets a court appoint a guardian ad litem in any case whenever the court deems it expedient to do so, even if Alex Doe already has a guardian or conservator of the estate who has already appeared on Alex Doe's behalf.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "When a minor, a person who lacks legal capacity to make decisions, or a person for whom a conservator has been appointed is a party, that person shall appear either by a guardian or conservator of the estate or by a guardian ad litem appointed by the court in which the action or proceeding is pending, or by a judge thereof, in each case."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 372(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Code Civ. Proc. § 372(a)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=372.)
  "A guardian ad litem may be appointed in any case when it is deemed by the court in which the action or proceeding is prosecuted, or by a judge thereof, expedient to appoint a guardian ad litem to represent the minor, person who lacks legal capacity to make decisions, or person for whom a conservator has been appointed, notwithstanding that the person may have a guardian or conservator of the estate and may have appeared by the guardian or conservator of the estate."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 372(a)(2)(A) (California Legislative Information text), Code Civ. Proc. § 372(a)(2)(A) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=372.)
  Known gap: Both citations are subdivisions of the same statutory section, Code Civ. Proc. § 372 — § 372(a)(1) and § 372(a)(2)(A) — not independently sourced provisions. Section 372(a)(1) states the mandatory rule (such a person "shall appear" only through one of these representatives); § 372(a)(2)(A) states the separate, discretionary "expedient" standard a court may use to appoint a guardian ad litem even over an existing guardian or conservator of the estate. The statute does not define "expedient"; that judgment is left to the court. This clause does not cover the additional showing the statute requires when a guardian or conservator of the estate already exists (covered in a separate clause) or the exceptions letting certain minors appear without a guardian ad litem in specific proceeding types (also covered separately).

WHO MAY BE APPOINTED, AND WHY THIS DIFFERS FROM AN EXISTING GUARDIAN OR CONSERVATOR OF THE ESTATE
California Code of Civil Procedure § 372(a)(1) recognizes two distinct kinds of representative who may appear for Alex Doe in litigation: an existing guardian or conservator of the estate, or a guardian ad litem appointed by the court specifically for that action or proceeding. When Alex Doe already has a guardian or conservator of the estate and an application is instead made to appoint a guardian ad litem, § 372(a)(2)(B) permits the court to grant that application only if the applicant gives the existing guardian or conservator of the estate notice and a copy of the application upon filing, the application discloses that guardian or conservator of the estate's existence, and the application states the reasons why that guardian or conservator of the estate is inadequate to represent Alex Doe's interests in the action. Under § 372(a)(2)(C), the existing guardian or conservator of the estate then has five court days from receiving that notice to file any opposition.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]

  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 372(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Code Civ. Proc. § 372(a)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=372.)
  "If application is made for appointment of a guardian ad litem for a person described in paragraph (1), and that person has a guardian or conservator of the estate, the application may be granted only if all of the following occur: (i) The applicant gives notice and a copy of the application to the guardian or conservator of the estate upon filing the application. (ii) The application discloses the existence of a guardian or conservator of the estate. (iii) The application sets forth the reasons why the guardian or conservator of the estate is inadequate to represent the interests of the proposed ward in the action."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 372(a)(2)(B) (California Legislative Information text), Code Civ. Proc. § 372(a)(2)(B) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=372.)
  "The guardian or conservator of the estate shall have five court days from receiving notice of the application to file any opposition to the application."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 372(a)(2)(C) (California Legislative Information text), Code Civ. Proc. § 372(a)(2)(C) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=372.)
  Known gap: Three citations here are subdivisions of the same statutory section, Code Civ. Proc. § 372 — § 372(a)(1), § 372(a)(2)(B), and § 372(a)(2)(C) — not independently sourced provisions. The notice-and-adequacy showing in § 372(a)(2)(B) applies only when the proposed ward already has a guardian or conservator of the estate; the statute does not state a comparable showing for a first appointment where no such guardian or conservator exists. This clause does not address how a court evaluates whether an existing guardian or conservator of the estate is "inadequate" — the statute does not define that term — or the procedure for the existing guardian or conservator of the estate's opposition beyond the five-court-day filing window.

WHO MAY APPLY, AND THE PRE-APPOINTMENT DISCLOSURE REQUIREMENT
California Code of Civil Procedure § 373 sets out who may apply for appointment of a guardian ad litem and when, depending on the proposed ward's role in the case. If the minor is the plaintiff, the appointment must be made before the summons is issued, on the minor's own application if the minor is 14 years of age or older, or, if the minor is younger, on the application of a relative or friend of the minor. If the minor is the defendant, appointment is made on the minor's own application if 14 or older and the minor applies within 10 days after service of the summons; if the minor is younger than 14, or neglects to apply, appointment is instead made on the application of a relative or friend of the minor, of any other party to the action, or by the court on its own motion. If the person needing a guardian ad litem is someone who lacks legal competence to make decisions rather than a minor, § 373(c) allows the application to be made by a relative or friend of that person, by any other party to the action or proceeding, or by the court on its own motion. Separately, before the court appoints a guardian ad litem under this chapter, § 372(d) requires the proposed guardian ad litem to disclose to the court and all parties any known actual or potential conflict of interest that would or might arise from the appointment, and any familial or affiliate relationship the proposed guardian ad litem has with any of the parties; § 372(e) requires the guardian ad litem to promptly disclose to the court any new conflict, or any potential conflict that becomes an actual conflict, discovered after appointment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "If the minor is the plaintiff the appointment must be made before the summons is issued, upon the application of the minor, if the minor is 14 years of age or older, or, if under that age, upon the application of a relative or friend of the minor."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 373(a) (California Legislative Information text), Code Civ. Proc. § 373(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=373.)
  "If the minor is the defendant, upon the application of the minor, if the minor is 14 years of age or older, and the minor applies within 10 days after the service of the summons, or, if under that age or if the minor neglects to apply, then upon the application of a relative or friend of the minor, or of any other party to the action, or by the court on its own motion."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 373(b) (California Legislative Information text), Code Civ. Proc. § 373(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=373.)
  "If the person lacking legal competence to make decisions is a party to an action or proceeding, upon the application of a relative or friend of the person lacking legal competence to make decisions, or of any other party to the action or proceeding, or by the court on its own motion."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 373(c) (California Legislative Information text), Code Civ. Proc. § 373(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=373.)
  "Before a court appoints a guardian ad litem pursuant to this chapter, a proposed guardian ad litem shall disclose both of the following to the court and all parties to the action or proceeding: (1) Any known actual or potential conflicts of interest that would or might arise from the appointment. (2) Any familial or affiliate relationship the proposed guardian ad litem has with any of the parties."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 372(d) (California Legislative Information text), Code Civ. Proc. § 372(d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=372.)
  "If a guardian ad litem becomes aware that a potential conflict of interest has become an actual conflict of interest or that a new potential or actual conflict of interest exists, the guardian ad litem shall promptly disclose the conflict of interest to the court."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 372(e) (California Legislative Information text), Code Civ. Proc. § 372(e) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=372.)
  Known gap: This clause draws on five subdivisions from two statutory sections. Three — § 373(a), § 373(b), and § 373(c) — are subdivisions of the same section, Code Civ. Proc. § 373, governing who may apply and by when; two others — § 372(d) and § 372(e) — are subdivisions of the separate section, Code Civ. Proc. § 372, governing conflict-of-interest disclosure. No additional independent source beyond each of those two sections was found for the points drawn from it. This clause does not cover the form the application must take, what it must state beyond the applicant's identity and timing, or the consequence of a proposed guardian ad litem's failure to disclose a conflict once discovered.

SCOPE OF A GUARDIAN AD LITEM'S AUTHORITY IN THE LITIGATION
Under California Code of Civil Procedure § 372(a)(3), a guardian or conservator of the estate or guardian ad litem appearing for Alex Doe has the power, with the approval of the court in which the action or proceeding is pending, to compromise the action, to agree to the order or judgment to be entered for or against Alex Doe, and to satisfy any judgment or order in Alex Doe's favor or to release or discharge Alex Doe's claim under that compromise. This authority is expressly tied to the pending action or proceeding and to court approval of the specific litigation decision — it is a narrower, case-bound role than the ongoing management of a person's care or property carried out by a general guardian of the person or a general guardian or conservator of the estate appointed in a separate probate guardianship or conservatorship proceeding, which is why § 372(a)(1) and § 372(a)(2) (addressed in separate clauses of this document) treat a guardian ad litem and an existing guardian or conservator of the estate as two distinct kinds of representative for the same person.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "The guardian or conservator of the estate or guardian ad litem so appearing for any minor, person who lacks legal capacity to make decisions, or person for whom a conservator has been appointed shall have power, with the approval of the court in which the action or proceeding is pending, to compromise the same, to agree to the order or judgment to be entered therein for or against the ward or conservatee, and to satisfy any judgment or order in favor of the ward or conservatee or release or discharge any claim of the ward or conservatee pursuant to that compromise."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 372(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text), Code Civ. Proc. § 372(a)(3) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=372.)
  Known gap: The quoted text is a single subdivision, Code Civ. Proc. § 372(a)(3); no additional independent source beyond § 372 itself was found describing the guardian ad litem's litigation powers. This clause describes only the powers § 372(a)(3) itself lists — compromising the action, agreeing to the judgment or order, and satisfying or releasing the resulting claim, all subject to court approval — and the statement that this is narrower than a general guardian's or conservator's ongoing authority is this document's characterization of how § 372(a)(1)-(2) structure the two roles, not itself a quoted statutory definition of "guardian of the person" or "guardian of the estate." This clause does not cover how money or property payable to the minor or incapacitated person under the compromise must be handled, which the statute states is governed by a separate Probate Code provision outside the scope of this document's verification.

EXCEPTIONS: WHEN A MINOR MAY APPEAR WITHOUT A GUARDIAN AD LITEM IN FAMILY-LAW AND PROTECTIVE-ORDER PROCEEDINGS
California Code of Civil Procedure § 372 itself carves out proceedings where a minor may appear without a guardian ad litem, notwithstanding the general rule. Under § 372(b)(1), a minor 12 years of age or older may appear in court without a guardian, counsel, or guardian ad litem to request or oppose specified protective orders, including a harassment injunction or restraining order under Code of Civil Procedure § 527.6, a workplace violence injunction or restraining order under Code of Civil Procedure § 527.8, a domestic violence protective order under Family Code Division 10 (commencing with § 6200), or a protective order under Family Code §§ 7710 and 7720; the court may still appoint a guardian ad litem to assist the minor in that proceeding if it does not delay the order. Under § 372(c)(1), a minor who is a parent of the child at issue may also appear without a guardian ad litem in family court proceedings under Family Code Part 3 (commencing with § 7600), in dependency proceedings, in guardianship proceedings for a minor child under the Probate Code, and in other child custody, visitation, or support proceedings — but § 372(c)(2) requires the court to appoint a guardian ad litem for that minor parent if the court finds the minor parent unable to understand the nature of the proceedings or to assist counsel in preparing the case.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Notwithstanding subdivision (a), a minor 12 years of age or older may appear in court without a guardian, counsel, or guardian ad litem, for the purpose of requesting or opposing a request for any of the following: (A) An injunction or temporary restraining order or both to prohibit harassment pursuant to Section 527.6. (B) An injunction or temporary restraining order or both against violence or a credible threat of violence in the workplace pursuant to Section 527.8. (C) A protective order pursuant to Division 10 (commencing with Section 6200) of the Family Code. (D) A protective order pursuant to Sections 7710 and 7720 of the Family Code."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 372(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Code Civ. Proc. § 372(b)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=372.)
  "Notwithstanding subdivision (a), a minor may appear in court without a guardian ad litem in the following proceedings if the minor is a parent of the child who is the subject of the proceedings: (A) Family court proceedings pursuant to Part 3 (commencing with Section 7600) of Division 12 of the Family Code. (B) Dependency proceedings pursuant to Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 200) of Part 1 of Division 2 of the Welfare and Institutions Code. (C) Guardianship proceedings for a minor child pursuant to Part 2 (commencing with Section 1500) of Division 4 of the Probate Code. (D) Any other proceedings concerning child custody, visitation, or support."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 372(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Code Civ. Proc. § 372(c)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=372.)
  "If the court finds that the minor parent is unable to understand the nature of the proceedings or to assist counsel in preparing the case, the court shall, upon its own motion or upon a motion by the minor parent or the minor parent’s counsel, appoint a guardian ad litem."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 372(c)(2) (California Legislative Information text), Code Civ. Proc. § 372(c)(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=372.)
  Known gap: Three citations here — § 372(b)(1), § 372(c)(1), and § 372(c)(2) — are subdivisions of the same statutory section, Code Civ. Proc. § 372, not independently sourced provisions; they were not separately verified against the cross-referenced Family Code sections (§§ 6200, 7710, 7720, and Part 3 commencing with § 7600) or the cross-referenced Welfare and Institutions Code juvenile dependency provisions, which this clause names only as the statute itself names them. This clause does not state what those cross-referenced Family Code or Welfare and Institutions Code proceedings themselves require; it states only that § 372 exempts a minor in the described role from needing a guardian ad litem in them, subject to the court's discretion to appoint one under § 372(b)(1) or its obligation to appoint one under § 372(c)(2). No separate, freestanding Family Code provision governing the guardian ad litem appointment mechanism itself — as distinct from these appearance exceptions — was located in the sections verified for this document.

APPLICATION FOR APPOINTMENT AS GUARDIAN AD LITEM
I, Jane Doe, apply to Superior Court of California, County of Los Angeles for the appointment of John Smith as guardian ad litem for Alex Doe in Case No. 24CV000000, pending in Los Angeles County. Alex Doe is a party to this action or proceeding and is a minor, a person who lacks legal capacity to make decisions, or a person for whom a conservator has been appointed, and so cannot appear in this action or proceeding without a guardian ad litem or an existing guardian or conservator of the estate. [If Alex Doe already has a guardian or conservator of the estate, describe here the existence of that guardian or conservator of the estate and the reasons this application contends that guardian or conservator of the estate is inadequate to represent Alex Doe's interests in this action, and attach proof that notice and a copy of this application were given to that guardian or conservator of the estate upon filing.] Proposed guardian ad litem John Smith discloses, in a separate declaration filed with this application, any known actual or potential conflict of interest with Alex Doe or any party to this action, and any familial or affiliate relationship with any party. I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing is true and correct.

SIGNATURE BLOCK AND PROPOSED ORDER APPOINTING GUARDIAN AD LITEM
Executed on January 1, 2026 at Los Angeles, California.

Signature of Jane Doe (Applicant): ☐ _________________________

Signature of John Smith (Proposed Guardian Ad Litem), consenting to serve: ☐ _________________________

[PROPOSED] ORDER APPOINTING GUARDIAN AD LITEM

The court having reviewed the foregoing application, IT IS ORDERED that John Smith is appointed guardian ad litem for Alex Doe in Case No. 24CV000000, Superior Court of California, County of Los Angeles, for purposes of this action or proceeding only.

Dated: _________________________  Judge/Judicial Officer: _________________________

[This information sheet, and the application and proposed-order text above, are prepared for use alongside an actual application for appointment of a guardian ad litem filed in California superior court under Code of Civil Procedure §§ 372-373. They do not themselves constitute, replace, or complete a filed application, and no guardian ad litem is appointed for Alex Doe until a court signs an order; only a court order can do that.]

Under § 372(b)(1), a minor 12 years of age or older may appear in court without a guardian, counsel, or guardian ad litem to request or oppose specified protective orders, including a harassment injunction or restraining order under Code of Civil Procedure § 527.6, a workplace violence injunction or restraining order under Code of Civil Procedure § 527.8, a domestic violence protective order under Family Code Division 10 (commencing with § 6200), or a protective order under Family Code §§ 7710 and 7720; the court may still appoint a guardian ad litem to assist the minor in that proceeding if it does not delay the order. Under § 372(c)(1), a minor who is a parent of the child at issue may also appear without a guardian ad litem in family court proceedings under Family Code Part 3 (commencing with § 7600), in dependency proceedings, in guardianship proceedings for a minor child under the Probate Code, and in other child custody, visitation, or support proceedings — but § 372(c)(2) requires the court to appoint a guardian ad litem for that minor parent if the court finds the minor parent unable to understand the nature of the proceedings or to assist counsel in preparing the case.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 372(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Notwithstanding subdivision (a), a minor 12 years of age or older may appear in court without a guardian, counsel, or guardian ad litem, for the purpose of requesting or opposing a request for any of the following: (A) An injunction or temporary restraining order or both to prohibit harassment pursuant to Section 527.6. (B) An injunction or temporary restraining order or both against violence or a credible threat of violence in the workplace pursuant to Section 527.8. (C) A protective order pursuant to Division 10 (commencing with Section 6200) of the Family Code. (D) A protective order pursuant to Sections 7710 and 7720 of the Family Code.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 372(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Notwithstanding subdivision (a), a minor may appear in court without a guardian ad litem in the following proceedings if the minor is a parent of the child who is the subject of the proceedings: (A) Family court proceedings pursuant to Part 3 (commencing with Section 7600) of Division 12 of the Family Code. (B) Dependency proceedings pursuant to Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 200) of Part 1 of Division 2 of the Welfare and Institutions Code. (C) Guardianship proceedings for a minor child pursuant to Part 2 (commencing with Section 1500) of Division 4 of the Probate Code. (D) Any other proceedings concerning child custody, visitation, or support.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 372(c)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: If the court finds that the minor parent is unable to understand the nature of the proceedings or to assist counsel in preparing the case, the court shall, upon its own motion or upon a motion by the minor parent or the minor parent’s counsel, appoint a guardian ad litem.

expectedJSON.gap: Three citations here — § 372(b)(1), § 372(c)(1), and § 372(c)(2) — are subdivisions of the same statutory section, Code Civ. Proc. § 372, not independently sourced provisions; they were not separately verified against the cross-referenced Family Code sections (§§ 6200, 7710, 7720, and Part 3 commencing with § 7600) or the cross-referenced Welfare and Institutions Code juvenile dependency provisions, which this clause names only as the statute itself names them. This clause does not state what those cross-referenced Family Code or Welfare and Institutions Code proceedings themselves require; it states only that § 372 exempts a minor in the described role from needing a guardian ad litem in them, subject to the court's discretion to appoint one under § 372(b)(1) or its obligation to appoint one under § 372(c)(2). No separate, freestanding Family Code provision governing the guardian ad litem appointment mechanism itself — as distinct from these appearance exceptions — was located in the sections verified for this document.
